findings.claim: The unit is named 'chemistry-paper-2' beside a sibling 'chemistry-paper-1', which implies a two-paper chemistry split.
findings.truth: J260 has ONE chemistry paper: Foundation J260/02 and Higher J260/06, each 95 marks, 1 hour 45 minutes, 26.4% of the GCSE, assessing C1-C6 plus BCP7 and BCP8. Papers 1-4 are Biology /01, Chemistry /02, Physics /03 and Combined /04 (75 marks, 1 hour 45 minutes, 20.8%); Papers 5-8 mirror them at Higher. The 'paper-1 / paper-2' split is Gateway-shaped, not J260. No lesson in this unit states a paper structure, a duration or a mark total, so nothing in the text is wrong and nothing should be renamed. Chapter mapping established from the spec and recorded here: L1 = C3.1 plus C4.2 (with C2.3 ionic recap), L2 = C3.2, L3 = C3.3, L4 = C3.4, L5 = C4.1 plus C4.4, L6 = C4.2, L7 = C4.3, L8 = C5.1. Nothing in this unit covers C1.1.1-4 (particle model) or C1.1.7-8 (combustion pollutants and air quality), the gap the sibling unit flagged; those remain taught in neither chemistry unit.
findings.evidence: spec Content Overview and Assessment Overview tables, both tiers; chapter headings C3, C4 and C5; lesson titles and content read in full

findings.claim: Assessable outcomes inside the chapters this unit covers (C3, C4, C5) are taught in neither chemistry unit.
findings.truth: Missing from both units: C3.4.6 and C3.4.7 (deduce and calculate empirical formulae - the word 'empirical' appears in no lesson of either unit); C4.3.3 and C4.3.4 (fullerenes, nanotubes, 'atoms in tubes or rings' - L7 teaches graphene only, and 'fullerene' and 'nanotube' appear nowhere); C4.3.6-C4.3.9 (estimate size and scale, standard form, ratios, calculate surface areas and volumes of cubes - the unit sets no numeric nanoparticle work at all); C4.4.1 with its two practicals (corrosion and rusting of iron, barrier and sacrificial protection - 'rust' and 'corrode' appear nowhere); C5.1.1 (formulations), C5.1.2 (scientific versus everyday 'pure'), C5.1.7 (crystallisation), C5.1.6b and 6c (aqueous and non-aqueous solvents, locating agents); C5.2.4-C5.2.10 (the mole, the Avogadro constant, reacting masses - all Higher) and the whole of C5.3 (concentration in g/dm3 and mol/dm3, neutralisation, titration technique and evaluation) - 'titration' appears in no lesson of either unit. Outside the covered chapters, the whole of C6 (acids and salts, rates of reaction, yield) has no home either, and PAG C4 (production of salts) and PAG C5 (measuring rates) are never mentioned. Recommendation: build one quantitative-chemistry lesson (C5.2 moles and reacting masses plus C5.3 concentration and titration), one C6 lesson on acids, salts, rates and yield, and fold rusting and corrosion prevention into L5 and fullerenes and nanotubes into L7.
findings.evidence: spec C3.4, C4.3, C4.4, C5.1, C5.2, C5.3, C6 outcome lists and PAG table; keyword sweep of all 16 chemistry lesson files in both units

findings.claim: L8 teaches flame tests for five metal ions, sodium hydroxide precipitate tests for six metal ions, carbonate, sulfate and halide tests, and instrumental methods (gas chromatography, mass spectrometry, GC-MS) as 'the tests you need to know'.
findings.truth: None of that is in J260 Combined Science B. C5.1 covers only formulations, purity and melting point data, chromatography with stationary and mobile phases and Rf values, and filtration, crystallisation, simple distillation and fractional distillation. The words 'flame test', 'precipitate' as an ion test, 'silver nitrate', 'barium' and 'limewater' do not appear in the spec, and neither does any instrumental method. The only ion test in the whole of J260 is C1.4.2, the chlorine test with blue litmus paper. Every fact in the out-of-spec material was checked and is correct (flame colours, all six hydroxide precipitate colours, the aluminium-versus-magnesium excess-NaOH distinction, the three halide precipitate colours, the acidification reagents, and Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O, which balances), so this is a scope problem and not a truth problem. The load is large: roughly 60% of the article, the description, practice questions 1, 2, 3 and 5, knowledge checks 1, 2, 3 and 5, and 10 of the 13 flashcards. Meanwhile four in-spec C5.1 outcomes get no coverage at all (formulations, scientific versus everyday 'pure', crystallisation, locating agents and non-aqueous solvents). Coordinator's ruling, 5 Sep 2026: option (a) is approved as a LABEL only, with no rebuild now. A 'Scope note' key-fact block is inserted as the first block of content_html, before the first heading, telling students that the flame tests, hydroxide precipitates, halide and sulfate tests and instrumental methods are not on this course, and that the chromatography and the chapter C5 tests are what they need. The block carries no data-narration-id, so narration blocks are unchanged, and it is one balanced key-fact div pair with its label div. The out-of-spec teaching itself is left in place as background; a full rebuild around C5.1 remains the longer-term fix.
findings.evidence: spec C5.1 outcomes 1-8 and the C5 chapter overview; spec keyword sweep (flame, precipitate, silver nitrate, barium, limewater, litmus); C1.4.2

findings.claim: 'methane (\ (CH_4\)) has a much lower boiling point than octane (\ (C_8H_{18}\))' - the KaTeX delimiters carry a space after the backslash.
findings.truth: \ ( is not a KaTeX delimiter, so both formulae render as the literal strings '\ (CH_4\)' and '\ (C_8H_{18}\)' on the page, and narration reads the backslashes and underscores aloud. Fixed to \(CH_4\) and \(C_8H_{18}\), matching the delimiter used everywhere else in this unit.
findings.evidence: KaTeX auto-render inline delimiter is \(...\); every other formula in this unit uses it correctly

findings.claim: Match knowledge check: 'Simple molecular' had to be paired with 'Does not conduct in any state', while 'Giant covalent (diamond)' was paired with 'Extremely hard, very high melting point'.
findings.truth: Diamond also does not conduct in any state - the lesson says so twice. A student who paired diamond with 'Does not conduct in any state' would be scientifically right and marked wrong. The simple-molecular option is now 'Low melting point, weak forces between molecules', which is true of simple molecular substances only.
findings.evidence: lesson content n13 and n17; the pairing order is unchanged

findings.claim: 'Most ionic compounds dissolve in water because water molecules can surround and pull away individual ions from the lattice.'
findings.truth: 'Most' overstates it. Many common ionic compounds are insoluble - calcium carbonate, barium sulfate, silver chloride and most metal hydroxides - and insolubility is the basis of precipitation chemistry in C6.1. Changed to 'Many'.
findings.evidence: settled fact (standard GCSE solubility rules); spec C6.1 precipitation

findings.claim: Practice question 1 reads 'Name the metal in the reactivity series that is used as a reference point for acid reactions' and its key is 'hydrogen'.
findings.truth: Hydrogen is not a metal, and the lesson's own first paragraph calls carbon and hydrogen 'non-metal reference points'. The stem contradicted the key and taught the misconception that hydrogen is a metal. Changed to 'Name the non-metal...', which makes the rubric line 'Developing: gives a metal name instead' work as intended.
findings.evidence: lesson content n2; spec C3.2.2 lists [hydrogen] in brackets among the metals for exactly this reason

findings.claim: The key for 'iron in copper sulfate solution' credits 'the blue solution turns pale green/colourless' and 'Secure: blue to colourless'.
findings.truth: Iron(II) sulfate solution is pale green, not colourless - the lesson's own text says so. Crediting 'colourless' rewards a wrong observation in a question that is entirely about the observation.
findings.evidence: lesson content n12; settled fact (Fe2+(aq) is pale green)

findings.claim: The key for 'Explain, in terms of electrons, why magnesium is more reactive than copper' credits 'magnesium's outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded, so they are held less strongly'.
findings.truth: That is false for this pair. Magnesium is 2,8,2 - its outer electrons are in shell 3. Copper is 2,8,18,1 - its outer electron is in shell 4, so it is further from the nucleus and more shielded, yet copper is far less reactive. The spec's reason is the tendency to form the positive ion: magnesium loses its two outer electrons much more easily than copper does. The key now says that.
findings.evidence: spec C3.2.2 ('related to the tendency of the metal to form its positive ion'); electron configurations of Mg and Cu

findings.claim: 'metals higher in the series lose electrons more readily because their outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner electron shells.'
findings.truth: This is a group trend applied to the whole reactivity series, where it does not hold - aluminium (3 shells) is above zinc (4 shells), and copper (4 shells) sits near the bottom. Replaced with the spec's own framing: metals higher in the series hold their outer electrons less strongly, so they lose them more readily.
findings.evidence: spec C3.2 narrative and outcome C3.2.2; electron configurations of Al, Zn and Cu

findings.claim: Match knowledge check offered 'Reduction with carbon' and 'Displacement or reduction with carbon' as two of the three right-hand options, for 'Zinc (below carbon)' and 'Copper (below carbon)'.
findings.truth: The two options overlap, so zinc and copper are interchangeable and a correct pairing can be marked wrong. The copper option is now 'Displacement from solution by a more reactive metal', which is a real extraction route for copper and is distinct from carbon reduction.
findings.evidence: spec C3.2.1 (displacement reactions with other metals) and C3.2.4 (carbon reduction, including zinc)

findings.claim: Phytoextraction, bioleaching and ionic equations are taught and tested with no tier flag: a collapsible correctly wrapped in higher-only, but also practice questions 4 and 5, flashcards 9, 10, 11 and 12, and conclusion takeaway n24, all outside the wrapper.
findings.truth: C3.2.6 ('evaluate alternative biological methods of metal extraction (bacterial and phytoextraction)') is bold in the spec, so Higher tier only, and so is the 'and ionic equations' clause of C3.2.3. The wrapper on the article section is right and is kept. The two practice questions and the takeaway now carry a '(Higher tier)' prefix and the four flashcards carry the tag at the end of the question.
findings.evidence: spec bold file, C3.2 outcomes 3 and 6 and the bold narrative paragraph on ionic equations and biological extraction

findings.claim: A higher-only wrapper covered the whole 'What Happens at the Electrodes' section, hiding paragraph n6 from Foundation students.
findings.truth: n6 is the core both-tier description: cations arrive at the cathode and gain electrons, anions arrive at the anode and lose electrons. That is C3.3.1 ('describe electrolysis in terms of the ions present and reactions at the electrodes') and C3.3.3, neither of which is bold, and the spec's both-tier narrative states it in the same words. Only the half equations that follow (C3.3.4) are bold. The wrapper opening was moved down so it now covers n7 to n9 only; div open and close counts are unchanged.
findings.evidence: spec bold file C3.3 outcomes 1-8: only 4 and 5 are bold

findings.claim: A second higher-only wrapper hid the whole worked example 'Predicting Electrolysis Products' (aqueous copper(II) sulfate with inert electrodes) from Foundation students.
findings.truth: Competing reactions in the electrolysis of aqueous solutions is C3.3.7, not bold, so it is examined at Foundation as well. The worked example is a single narration block and cannot be split without adding a block, so the wrapper was removed and the two half-equation lines at the end of it - the only Higher-tier part - now read 'Half equation at cathode (Higher tier)' and 'Half equation at anode (Higher tier)'. Both half equations were recomputed and balance: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu, and 4OH- -> 2H2O + O2 + 4e- (O 4 = 4, H 4 = 4, charge -4 = -4). Div open and close counts are unchanged.
findings.evidence: spec bold file C3.3.7 (not bold) and C3.3.4 (bold); recomputation of both half equations

findings.claim: The mark scheme for the lead bromide half equation contained raw LaTeX: '\(Pb^{2+}(l) + 2e^- \rightarrow Pb(l)\)'.
findings.truth: Practice mark schemes are plain-text fields and are not passed through KaTeX, so the delimiters and the backslash commands render literally. Rewritten in unicode as Pb2+(l) + 2e- -> Pb(l) (with superscript characters). The equation itself is correct and balances.
findings.evidence: house rule: plain-text fields use unicode, *_html fields use entities; recomputation of the half equation

findings.claim: Practice question 6 (write a half equation), knowledge checks 3 and 5 and flashcard 12 (OIL RIG) test Higher-tier-only outcomes with no tier flag.
findings.truth: C3.3.4 ('write half equations') and C3.3.5 ('explain reduction and oxidation in terms of gain or loss of electrons, identifying which species are oxidised and which are reduced') are both bold. The three question items now carry a '(Higher tier)' prefix and the flashcard carries the tag at the end. Practice questions 1 and 2 and knowledge checks 1, 2 and 4 were checked and left alone: they are answerable from the both-tier outcomes C3.3.1 to C3.3.3 and from the both-tier key fact in the article.
findings.evidence: spec bold file C3.3 outcomes 4 and 5

findings.claim: The dodecane cracking mark scheme contained raw LaTeX '\(C_{12}H_{26} \rightarrow C_{10}H_{22} + C_2H_4\)'.
findings.truth: Rewritten in unicode. The chemistry is right: C 12 = 10 + 2 and H 26 = 22 + 4, so the equation balances. Every other cracking equation in the lesson was recomputed too - C10H22 -> C8H18 + C2H4 (C 10 = 10, H 22 = 22) and the worked example C10H22 -> C3H6 + C7H16 (C 10 = 10, H 22 = 22, and 2 x 7 + 2 = 16 for heptane) - and both are correct.
findings.evidence: house plain-text rule; recomputation of all three cracking equations

findings.claim: The six-mark sustainability mark scheme credits 'role of increased atom economy'.
findings.truth: Atom economy appears nowhere in the J260 Combined Science B spec. C6.3 treats yield qualitatively only and there is no atom-economy outcome at either tier. The phrase was removed; the rest of the key is in scope.
findings.evidence: spec keyword sweep ('economy' returns no outcome); spec C6.3 outcome list

findings.claim: The lesson teaches the bromine water test for alkenes in the article (n16) and in flashcard 9.
findings.truth: The bromine water test is not in J260 Combined Science B - alkenes appear only in the C3.4 narrative as a product of cracking, with no test outcome. It is correct chemistry and standard enrichment, so no edit; recorded so a future rebuild knows it is not assessed on this spec.
findings.evidence: spec keyword sweep ('bromine water' and 'alkene'); spec C3.4 outcome list

findings.claim: Practice question 1 mark scheme reads 'Award 1 mark for any one correct property', and the stem asks for TWO properties on a question typed as one mark.
findings.truth: 'Award N marks for' is a banned board rubric phrase; the house validator rejects the whole unit on it. The stem also contradicted its own rubric. The stem now asks for one property and the rubric reads 'Mastering: any one of: ...' and ends '[1 mark]'.
findings.evidence: house banned-string list; internal contradiction between stem, type and rubric

findings.claim: The match stem reads 'Match each disposal route to its environmental benefit', but one of the options is 'Worst option - materials lost and land used'.
findings.truth: Landfill has no environmental benefit, so the stem promised something the options do not deliver. Stem changed to 'Match each disposal route to the correct description:'. The pairings themselves were checked and are right.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction between stem and options

findings.claim: Practice question 1 mark scheme reads 'Award 1 mark for any answer stating that diamond has more/stronger bonds or a 3D network'.
findings.truth: 'Award N marks for' is a banned board rubric phrase and the house validator rejects the whole unit on it. Rewritten as 'Accept any answer stating that diamond has more bonds per carbon or a rigid three-dimensional network', with '[1 mark]' at the end. 'more/stronger bonds' was also loosened to 'more bonds per carbon' - the C-C covalent bonds in graphite are not weaker than those in diamond, they are fewer per atom.
findings.evidence: house banned-string list; settled fact (carbon-carbon bonds within a graphite layer are shorter and stronger than in diamond)

findings.claim: The match knowledge check pairs graphite with 'Layered hexagonal structure with delocalised electrons between layers'.
findings.truth: The lesson says the opposite three times: n13 says one electron per carbon is delocalised 'within each layer', the key fact repeats it, and the exam tip explicitly warns students to say conduction happens along the layers, not across them. Conduction in graphite is anisotropic and runs within the layers. Changed to 'within each layer'.
findings.evidence: lesson content n13, key fact n15 and exam tip n17; settled fact (graphite conducts along the layers)

findings.claim: L6 builds a whole section, a key fact, two practice questions, two knowledge checks, three flashcards and a takeaway on thermosoftening versus thermosetting polymers and covalent cross-linking.
findings.truth: The words 'thermoset', 'thermosoftening', 'cross-link' and 'tensile' appear nowhere in the J260 spec. The underlying science is legitimate for C4.2.4 ('the nature and arrangement of chemical bonds in polymers with reference to their properties') and C4.1.1 ('softening temperature (for polymers)'), and it is correct chemistry, so no edit. Recorded because roughly half of this lesson's questions drill terminology the paper will not use.
findings.evidence: spec keyword sweep; spec C4.1.1 and C4.2.4 outcome wording

findings.claim: The inline glossary and the glossary list define 'toxicity levels' as 'The concentration of a substance that is lethal to 50% of a test population under specified conditions, used to compare toxicity.'
findings.truth: That is the definition of LD50 or LC50, a specific measure, not of 'toxicity levels', which is the general phrase used in the sentence it annotates. Replaced in both places with 'How poisonous a substance is: the amount or concentration needed to cause harm to a living organism.'
findings.evidence: settled fact (LD50 / LC50 definition); the sentence the dfn annotates uses the phrase generally

findings.claim: The nanoparticle dfn reads 'where 1 nm = 10−9 m.'
findings.truth: The exponent has lost its superscript, so the tooltip reads '1 nm = 10-9 m'. The glossary list already carries the correct 10 to the power minus 9 in unicode; the dfn now matches it.
findings.evidence: internal inconsistency with the lesson's own glossary_terms entry

findings.claim: Flashcard 8 reads 'What is the answer to: Graphene is made of a single layer of what element arranged in a hexagonal lattice?'
findings.truth: 'What is the answer to:' is a drafting artefact, almost certainly added to satisfy the single-word-answer rule. Rewritten as 'What element is graphene made of, arranged in a hexagonal lattice?', which still opens with 'What' and still passes the validator.
findings.evidence: house flashcard rules (FC_SINGLE_WORD_OK_Q); validator re-run after the edit

findings.claim: All four gas formulae in the gas-test list are written with a space in the KaTeX delimiter: '\ (H_2\)', '\ (O_2\)', '\ (CO_2\)', '\ (Cl_2\)'.
findings.truth: \ ( is not a delimiter, so all four render as literal backslash-and-underscore strings and narration reads them aloud. Fixed to \(H_2\), \(O_2\), \(CO_2\) and \(Cl_2\), matching the correctly formed formulae later in the same lesson.
findings.evidence: KaTeX auto-render inline delimiter is \(...\); the same lesson forms \(Ca^{2+}\) and \(BaSO_4\) correctly

findings.claim: Zinc extraction is written as 2ZnO(s) + C(s) -> 2Zn(l) + CO2(g).
findings.truth: The equation balances (Zn 2 = 2, O 2 = 2, C 1 = 1) and the spec gives no equation for it, so no edit. Industrially the smelting temperature is above zinc's boiling point of 907 degrees C, so zinc leaves as a vapour and is condensed; (g) would be the more accurate state symbol. (l) is the usual GCSE simplification and is not mark-affecting on this spec.
findings.evidence: spec C3.2.4 names zinc extraction but gives no equation; settled fact (boiling point of zinc)

findings.claim: Tier audit of the six candidates named in the brief, checked against the bold-preserved spec extraction.
findings.truth: Bold, so Higher tier only: half equations and the electron definition of oxidation and reduction (C3.3.4 and C3.3.5, also C4.4.2), ionic equations (the bold clause of C3.2.3), biological metal extraction (C3.2.6), and moles and reacting masses (C5.2.4-C5.2.7, C5.2.9) - the last of these is taught nowhere in the unit, so there was nothing to wrap. NOT bold, so both tiers and correctly left unwrapped: reactivity explained in terms of the tendency to form a positive ion (C3.2.2), life-cycle assessment reasoning in all its parts (C4.4.3-C4.4.6), chromatography and Rf calculation (C5.1.5), and every nanoparticle surface-area and ratio outcome (C4.3.2, C4.3.3, C4.3.8, C4.3.9). Two wrappers were found in the wrong direction, both in L3, and are fixed under F13 and F14.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/combined-science-b-21c-J260-bold.md, chapters C3, C4 and C5 outcome tables

summary: Eight lessons checked against OCR Twenty First Century Science B J260 (Combined). Thirty findings: 27 lesson-level and 3 unit-level; 24 FIX (40 edits), 2 ADJUDICATE, 4 NOTE. Four HIGH. Three are fixed: two banned 'Award 1 mark for' rubrics (L5, L6) that fail the house validator for the whole unit, and an L2 mark scheme that rewarded a false electron-shielding reason for magnesium being more reactive than copper. The fourth is L8, which is built mostly on flame tests, hydroxide precipitate tests, halide and sulfate tests and GC-MS, none of which is in J260; on the coordinator ruling of 5 Sep it is labelled with a scope note rather than rebuilt. Two higher-only wrappers in L3 ran the wrong way and hid both-tier electrolysis content from Foundation; ten question items across L2 and L3 plus one conclusion takeaway now carry a '(Higher tier)' tag for genuinely bold outcomes. Every equation, half equation, cracking calculation and Rf value in the unit was recomputed and all were correct.
